activities.anchor: It does not say your choices don't matter
activities.caption: true or false — what determinism does not claim
activities.name: fwDeterminismJudge

statements.s: Determinism renders deliberation causally idle — what you think makes no difference to what happens.
statements.why: Your deliberations are links in the causal chain, and may be exactly what produces the outcome.

statements.s: Determinism means the future is written down somewhere, independent of what anyone does.
statements.why: That sense of "predetermined" is exactly what the thesis does not claim.

statements.s: Even in a largely deterministic world, next month's weather may be impossible to forecast.
statements.why: Real systems are usually too complicated to compute — fixing the future is not the same as predicting it.

statements.s: Laplace's demon is a definition of what the laws would imply, not an engineering roadmap.
statements.why: Perfect prediction would require knowledge no observer inside the universe can have.

activities.anchor: The two are opposites on the point that matters
activities.caption: drag the divider — determinism versus fatalism
activities.name: fwFatalCompare

config.prompt: Drag the divider — the distinction the whole debate leans on:

before.label: Determinism
before.text: You will be saved because you visited the doctor — and had you not, the future would have differed. Your efforts are causally effective, indeed necessary.

after.label: Fatalism
after.text: The doctor will save you regardless of whether you visit her — whatever will be, will be.

config.why: Opposites exactly here: determinism makes your efforts necessary links; fatalism makes them irrelevant.

config.q: Quantum mechanics makes outcomes at the smallest scales genuinely probabilistic. Does that rescue free will?
choices: No — a random choice is no more yours than a determined one
config.why: Randomness is not control — imagine a machine injecting pure noise into your decisions: a slot machine in the skull. The dilemma stands: determined feels unfree, random feels unfree.

activities.anchor: God doesn't "foresee" your choice, God simply sees it
activities.caption: pair the foreknowledge moves
activities.name: fwBoethiusMatch

config.prompt: The debate's oldest form — pair each move with its content:

pairs.right: God already knows what you will do tomorrow — so you cannot do anything else
God is timeless, outside the flow of time — watching does not force the bird
existing within time, moment by moment, the argument bites harder
perfect prediction replaces perfect laws — the question is the same as the scientific one

config.why: Divine foreknowledge and human freedom — structurally identical to the modern problem, which is why this lesson belongs to the philosophy of God as much as of mind.

config.root: The hard determinist says desert-based reactions misfire. Can we put them down?

start.text: You learn hard determinism is true. Your friend betrays you. What happens to the resentment?

choices.label: It misfires — drop the desert version
choices.feedback: The hard determinist's line: punishment as deserved suffering goes the way of public flogging.

choices.label: It arrives anyway — theory meets temperament
choices.feedback: P. F. Strawson's 1962 reply: reactive emotions are not optional equipment we can put down once we believe a theory.

drop.text: Whether hard determinism is livable is itself a live philosophical question — the cost its opponents press hard.

strawson.text: Gratitude and resentment are built into ordinary moral life; a theory demanding their extinction may be asking for the psychologically impossible.

config.why: The view has an uncomfortable cost: ordinary moral life seems to collapse — praise, anger, forgiveness all presuppose desert.

activities.anchor: a short, sharp argument published by Peter van Inwagen in 1983
activities.caption: rebuild the consequence argument
activities.name: fwConsequenceOrder

items: Nobody has power over the laws of nature
Nobody has power over the state of the world in the distant past
If determinism is true, our present actions are an inevitable consequence of laws plus past
No power over X, no power over Y, and X and Y jointly entail Z — no power over Z
So nobody has power over their own present actions
config.why: The premises feel almost undeniable — which is why the compatibilist escapes by arguing the conclusion does not mean what it seems to mean, not by denying the argument.

activities.caption: guess the share — the profession's verdict
activities.name: fwPhilPapersEstimate

config.prompt: Compatibilism is the majority position among professional philosophers. Roughly what share took a compatibilist line in the 2020 PhilPapers survey?
config.why: About 59% — the majority view. Freedom worth having is the capacity to respond to reasons, foresee consequences and act on your own evaluations — abilities that exist in a determined world.

activities.anchor: are routinely cited as disproving free will
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the Libet headlines
activities.name: fwLibetSpot

config.prompt: One line of this gloss on the Libet experiments is wrong — click it:
lines: Libet's 1983 experiments disproved free will: the brain decides before the conscious mind does.
Participants watching a fast clock reported deciding to move at about 200 ms.
A readiness potential — a build-up of brain activity — preceded their report by over half a second.
Libet himself proposed a "free won't" — a conscious veto — to rescue some role for the agent.
Later work (Schurger and colleagues, 2012) suggests the readiness potential may be ordinary background noise crossing a threshold.
config.correction: They showed a brain signal preceding a reported decision in a highly artificial task — spontaneous finger flexions, not deliberative choice. They settle nothing about the argument between determinist and compatibilist.
config.why: The experiments constrain certain pictures of the mind; the debate was never about millisecond timings.
